docs.text: DNS Summary A speed dial app of the Internet, contains mapping of websites names to IP address - don't need to memorize IP addresses What this is Domain Name System (DNS) servers store databases that contain mappings to websites' respective IP addresses How it works (high-level) Your devices is configured to point to a DNS server when a domain name is entered into web browser The device fetch the IP address from DNS server & route the traffic to that IP address Usually, the selected DNS server is on your local network, but it doesn't have to be Common pitfalls / misunderstandings Misconception 1 Misconception 2 Misuse or overgeneralization Issues with DNS DNS has no native ability to distinguish legitimate and malicious network traffic, will allow users to access websites even if it's compromised or contains malware An infected computer may change its DNS server to point to malicious ones, directing to harmful domains by attackers DNS sinkhole is mean to mitigate these situations Related concepts DNS sinkhole References catchpoint DNS network guide

docs.text: IP Addresses Summary An IP address identifies devices on a network; can be dynamic or static. What this is A unique numerical label assigned to each device connected to a computer network that uses the Internet Protocol for communication Allow to identify a device on the network & locate the dvice to enable communications with other devices Components of an IP address Network Portion: Identifies the network to which the device belongs Host Portion: Identifies the individual device on the network Subnet Mask (for IPv4): Defines which parts of the IP is the network and which part is host Example: IP 192.168.1.10 with subnet mask 255.255 255.0 Network ID: 192.168.1.0 Host ID: 10 How does it work Alice & Bob wants to communicate, both uses their router public IP address provided by their ISPs Alice sends Bob a message via email, which is broken down into smaller packets, including Alice's public IP & Bob's mail server's public IP The packets are sent to Alice's email client and it is forwarded to a series of routers to until it arrives at Bob's email server' Bob can now make a request to the server to view the content via his public IP address The server sends the email to Bob's device Type of IP Address Public & Private IP address Public IP addresses: Assigned to every device diretly connected to the Internet Unique across the entire Internet Assigned by Internet Service Providers (ISPs) Example: Web servers, email servers Private IP addresses: Used within privste networks, not routable on the Internet Unique within their own network Used for communication between devices in the same network Example: Home networks, corporate networks IPv4 & IPv6 IPv4: 32-bit adddress, represented in dotted-decimal format i.e 185.102.12.253 Consists of four octets (8 bits each) But have limited address space (~4.3 billion addresses) IPv6: 128-bit address, represented in hexadecimal format i.e 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 Consists of eight groups of four hexadecimal digits Vastly larger address space (340 undecillion addresses) Designed to address the limitations of IPv4 and support the growing number of internet-connected devices Static & Dynamic IP address Static IP addresses are permanently assigned to devices i.e servers, websites that need a constant address Dynamic IP addresses are temporarily assigned by DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol), used for devices that don't require permanent addresses Unicaset, Broadcast, Multicast & Anycast Unicast: One-to-one communication where data is sent from one device to another specific device i.e web browsing, file transfers (FTP), emails (SMTP)...etc Broadcast: One-to-all communication where data is sent from one device to all devices on the network i.e Network discovery, DHCP requests, ARP requests...etc Multicast: One-to-many communication where data is sent from one device to a specific group of devices on the network i.e streaming, video conferencing, online gaming...etc Anycast: One-to-one-of-many communication where data is sent to the nearest device in a group of devices (based on distance) i.e CDN (Content Delivery Networks) routing, DNS services...etc Other special IP addresses Loopback addresses (e.g., 127.0.0.1 for IPv4, ::1 for IPv6) are used for local testing and communication within a device i.e sending data to yourself Broadcast addresses (e.g., 255.255.255.255 for IPv4) are used to send messages to all devices on a network Multicast addresses are used to send messages to a specific group of devices on a network Why it matters (security perspective) IP Spoofing: Attackers can disguise their IP address to appear as a trusted source to bypass security & gain unauthorized access to systems Geolocation Tracking: IP addresses can be used to track users' physical locations, raising privacy DDOS Attacks: Attackers can use multiple IP addresses to overwhelm a target system with traffic, causing service disruptions Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attacks: Attackers can intercept communications between two parties by exploiting vulnerabilities in IP routing Port Scanning: Attackers can use IP addresses to identify open ports on a target system, which can be exploited for unauthorized access Prevention/Mitigation Use VPNS to mask real IP addresses by re-routing internet traffic through a secure server Use a proxy server to act as an intermediary between the user and the internet, hiding the user's real IP address Implement firewalls to monitor and control incoming/outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules Use Tor browser as Tor network routes your data through multiple volunteer-operated servers (nodes), masking your IP address and encrypting your traffic Related concepts Subnetting NAT (Network Address Translation) DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) References geeks4geeks

docs.text: Subnetting Summary Subnetting is dividing a large network into smaller sub-networks, called subnets Each subnets allowed devices to talk efficiently and improve network performance, security and management What this is The process of splitting up one IP network into smaller IP networks Done via subnet mask/ CIDR prefix to decide which bits of an IP address represent the network and host Tackling scale + control, allow to organize IP address and reduce unnecessary local traffic & supporting segmentation 8 attributes of subnetting Network ID: First IP address in each sub-network Unique purpose - not allow to assign to users Allow routers to identify subnet along with CIDR/subnet mask Broadcast IP: Last IP address in each sub-network Unique purpose - not allow to assign to users Used to communicate with all IP addresses in sub-network First Host IP: First host IP address after Network ID Last Host IP: Last host IP address before Broadcast IP Host IP: The IP address assigned to the user Next Network: The network ID of the next Sub-Network No. IP addresses: Number of IP addresses in sub-network CIDR(Classless Inter-Domain Routing)/Subnet-mask: Alt ways to identify size of subnet Example: A subnet mask /24 means the first 24 bits (left to right) are part of the network ID, and the rest are the host ID 255.255.255.0 = 11111111.11111111.11111111.00000000 Network ID: 192.168.1.0 Broadcast IP: 192.168.1.255 Host IP: 192.168.1.1 --> 192.168.1.254 Example: A subnet mask of /26 would mean that 255.255.255.192 = 11111111.11111111.11111111.11000000 Network ID: 192.168.1.0 Broadcast IP: 192.168.1.63 Host IP: 192.168.1.1 → 192.168.1.62 Subnet Mask vs CIDR A subnet mask is a 32-bit number used in IP addressing to seperate the network portion from host portion Allow devices to determine which part of an IP address refers to the network they're present & which part refer to specific location within that network CIDR Notation uses a simple format which make it easier to read The number after the slash (/n) represents num of bits used for the network portion of the IP address How it works (high-level) Conceptual explanation only. No commands, no configs. Use diagrams if needed. Why it matters (security perspective) Enables a single IP network to be divided into smaller logical network --> More efficient IP address usage Improved security (segmentation) as subnets isolate departments, preventing unauthorized access Easier maintenance due to smaller segmented networks Can prioritize traffic to different subnets Can lead to more complexitiy and higher cost due to increase in routers, communication layers and careful planning Each subnet wastes 2 IP addresses, being network ID and broadcast IP Common pitfalls / misunderstandings Subnetting only divides and segment the networks, it doesn't delete or remove the addresses Example: 192.168.1.0/26 still have all 256 addresses, but has been divided into 4 subnets To work out how many subnets, we have 2 bits to used for the subnet & 6 bits (64 values) for the host IPs The 2 bits are 128, 64 and there are 4 values: 00,01,10,11 Related concepts Concept A Concept B References

docs.text: DNS Sinkhole Summary A DNS sinkhole is used to blocked malicious DNS request What this is Works by intercepting DNS queries, compare them to dynamic list of known malicious domains If query attempts resolve to a bad domain, then route the traffic to a null route How it works (high-level) For general malicious/fishy websites For example, there's a known bad website called malware.com points to 1.1.1.1 To stop traffic from coming there, we configure our DNS server to point to 127.0.0.1 (our local IP address) if receives a query from malware.com For advertisements Your device queries a DNS server to resolve domain names into IP address However, websites also load third party ads and trackers, requiring additional DNS lookups to advertisers domains A configured DNS sinkhole allow us to intercept and block the unwanted queries, returning a null IP address to our browser Issues with DNS Sinkhole Won't block all ads or malcious websites, ONLY stops DNS-based threats Potential false positives or incompelete database of malicious/ads sites No native alerting Related concepts DNS References Blog post on removing ads through DNS sinkhole catchpoint DNS network guide

docs.text: YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) Definition: A human-readable data serialization language used for config files and data exchange. Applications : - Allow humans to easily read or create config files - Typically store things a program would need at run time, without needing to hard code the values ELIF: A general file format to store structured data that's way more readable to humans Do not confuse with: - YAML is a superset of JSON, technically a YAML parser can understand JSON - YAML is more easily readable by humans while JSON has a more rigid structure Example: key: value list: - item1 - item2 JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) Definition: A light-weight format for storing and transporting data. Syntactically identical to the code for creating JavaScript objects as it derives from JavaScript Application: - Often used for light-weight data exchange between APIs and web servers - Storing config settings - Used in security tokens JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) for authentication purposes ELIF: A way to store data in text in an organized way instead of XML or binary formats Example: { "id": 1, "name": "Example Item", "enabled": true, "count": 3, "tags": [ "example", "demo" ], "details": { "owner": "Alice", "priority": "medium" } } XML (eXtensible Markup Language) Definition: A language/file structure designed to store and transport data ELIF: Basically HTML but it doesn't do ANYTHING, just information wrapped in tags Application: - XML was designed to carry data, not display them unlike HTML - XML tags and document structure must be defined manually by users - Stores data in plain text format, providing a software & hardware independent way of storing, transporting and sharing data Do not confuse with: HTML Static Definition in Java context: The static members (variable, methods, nested class) belongs to the class itself, not to any specific object (instance) of that class. Definition in website context: Describe pages with fixed content that appears the same to every user, without any real-time, server side processing or interaction with database Definition in IP address context: An IP address that does not change frequently. Used in cases of hosting, web servers and secure communications Base64 Definition: A binary-to-text encoding that uses 64 printable characters, with each character represents 6 bits to maintain integrity of data ELIF: A way of transforming data into clean, safe data that will make sure data does not get change passing through systems Application: - Includes upper/lowercase English letters, digits 0-9 & plus (+) and forward slash (/) - Makes data 33% larger in memory usage, should only use when necessary - Does not contain special characters that might be interpret as special commands - Ensure data doesn't get corrupted when systems expect clean readable texts - Note safe for URL Base32 Definition: A binary-to-text encoding that uses 32 printable chracters, each character are 5 bits in length ELIF: Same shit like Base64 but less bits used Application: - Allow data to be passed to a system that accepts single-byte character input, or UTF-8 encoded string input or appended to a URL without being mangled - Use in URLs as Base64 have those troubling symbols and may be treated specially Parsing Definition: The process of analyzing a sequence of data (string/bytes) into its components (tokens) for computers to work with reliably ELIF: Turning some kind of data into another kind of data but with structures Application: - Apply grammar to tokens to build structure Do not confuse with: - Parsing is not transforming one thing into another, that's the job of the compiler. Parsing is one of the step to compile a program - Parsing does not extract meaning from a text, that's semantic analysis, a step of the compiling process Tokenization Definition: Breaking down stream of characters into smaller, meaningful units called tokens ELIF: Application: - After broken down into tokens --> pass through parser - Part of the broader process of processing raw inputs into structured meaning that your program can work with - Use case in compilers, intepreters, data deserialization, protocol message decoding VPN (Virtual Private Network) Definition: A private network that you can access from anywhere through an encrypted tunnel ELIF: Establish a tunnel between VPN server and you, and send the traffic through there, which the VPN will forward to your intended destination Application: - Can allow you to access restricted content, depending where VPN server is located - Self-host VPNs, allow to access network over the internet securely - If on HTTP, then allow to protect sensitive data and personal informationAllow to work remotely over the internet Virtual Environment Definition: One-line definition.
